history.heading: Ancient and medieval history
paragraphs: The territory of Azerbaijan, between the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus Mountains, has been inhabited since prehistoric times; the rock carvings of Gobustan date back tens of thousands of years. In antiquity the region was home to Caucasian Albania and was influenced by Persian empires. Zoroastrianism was important, and natural gas fires gave rise to the name "Land of Fire".

Arab conquests in the 7th century brought Islam. From the 11th century, Oghuz Turkic tribes migrated into the region, gradually making Turkic the dominant language. Local states such as the Shirvanshahs flourished, and the region was later ruled by the Safavids, a dynasty with roots in Azerbaijan, and other Persian dynasties.

history.heading: Russian rule and oil
paragraphs: The Russian Empire conquered the northern part of the region in the early 19th century, and the 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay divided Azerbaijani-populated lands between Russia and Persia; many Azerbaijanis still live in Iran.
In the late 19th century Baku became the site of one of the world's first oil booms, producing about half of the world's oil around 1900 and attracting investors such as the Nobel brothers.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, proclaimed in 1918, was one of the first democratic republics in the Muslim world and granted women the vote, but it was conquered by the Bolsheviks in 1920. Azerbaijan became a Soviet republic.

Conflict over Nagorno-Karabakh erupted in 1988. After independence in 1991, war with Armenia ended in 1994 with Armenian forces controlling the region and surrounding districts, and hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis displaced. Heydar Aliyev took power in 1993; his son Ilham Aliyev succeeded him in 2003. Azerbaijan regained territory in a 2020 war and took full control of Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Azerbaijani, a Turkic language closely related to Turkish, is the official language, written in the Latin alphabet since 1991. Russian is also widely understood. Most people are Muslim, mainly Shia, but society is largely secular.
Nowruz, the spring New Year, is the most beloved holiday, celebrated with bonfires and special sweets such as shekerbura and pakhlava.

culture.heading: Music and arts
paragraphs: Mugham, a complex form of improvised classical music, and the ashiq tradition of poet-musicians are recognised by UNESCO. Uzeyir Hajibeyov composed the first opera in the Muslim world, Leyli and Majnun, in 1908. Carpet weaving is a renowned art.
The 12th-century poet Nizami Ganjavi, who wrote in Persian, is a national icon. The Old City of Baku, with the Maiden Tower and Palace of the Shirvanshahs, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

culture.heading: Food
paragraphs: Plov (rice pilaf) is the centrepiece of many meals, alongside dolma, kebabs, dushbara dumplings and the yogurt soup dovgha. Tea is served in pear-shaped glasses and is central to hospitality.

politics.heading: Strong presidency
paragraphs: Azerbaijan is formally a presidential republic, but power is highly concentrated in the president, and the Aliyev family has led the country since 1993. Constitutional changes removed term limits and created the post of first vice-president, held by the president's wife.

Elections are not considered free by international observers, and opposition figures, journalists and activists face restrictions and imprisonment. The ruling New Azerbaijan Party dominates parliament.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Azerbaijan pursues a balanced foreign policy. It has a very close alliance with Türkiye, strong ties with Israel, energy partnerships with the European Union and complex relations with Russia and Iran.
Peace with Armenia, including border demarcation and transport links, is a major issue; the two countries agreed a peace treaty text in 2025.

economy.heading: Oil and gas
paragraphs: Oil and natural gas dominate the economy, accounting for most exports and a large share of state revenue. Pipelines such as the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan oil pipeline and the Southern Gas Corridor carry Caspian energy to Türkiye and Europe without passing through Russia.
A sovereign wealth fund, SOFAZ, manages oil revenues. Baku's modern skyline, including the Flame Towers, reflects oil wealth.

economy.heading: Diversification
paragraphs: The government aims to diversify through agriculture, tourism, transport links on the Middle Corridor between China and Europe, and renewable energy. Reconstruction of the regions regained from Armenian control is a major state project. The currency is the manat.
